newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa fiscal deficit worse than thought -report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa fiscal deficit worse than thought -report.

text.p: South Africa's fiscal deficit is far worse than generally thought because headline measurements of the size of public sector borrowing exclude key components of state spending, a report on Wednesday said.
Cape Town-based BOE Asset Management said in its latest Investment Outlook that the true central government budget deficit in 1995/96 (April-March) was 7.1 percent of GDP rather than 5.8 percent.
For the the current fiscal year, the deficit was likely to actually grow to around 7.6 percent, contrary to official forecasts that it will narrow to 5.1 percent, it said.
Adding in the borrowing of provincial and local government gives a possible total public sector borrowing requirement of more than eight percent for the current year.

Analyst Rob Lee said the main missing elements in calculating public borrowing were the losses on the forward cover book of the Reserve bank and the large discounts at which government stock is issued.
"The true size of the State's demand on the economy is generally being underestimated...Furthermore, these deficits are not falling, as commonly thought, but rising," Lee said.
"On the basis of this data South Africa appears dangerously close to being in the debt trap, if it is not there already."
Forex loss on the central bank's forward cover book in 1996/97 will total 5.0 billion rand, and recent rand weakness may result in additional losses, he said.
At the same time the total discount on government stock issued will be 8.5 bilion rand, while the amortised discount should rise to about 4.0 billion, he added.
In the first four months of the year the total discounts on newly issued stock were almost 3.0 billion, according to the Reserve Bank.
As a result, Lee said real interest rates would remain very high with little chance of a decline next year, as widely expected.
The sustainability of single-digit inflation was also highly questionable given continued deficits of this scale.
"If and when foreign investors perceive South Africa's fiscal position in this light prospects of attracting a significant ongoing flow of foreign capital will further recede," Lee said.
His report recommended a five-point action plan:
- more stringent cuts in public spending;
- an increase in value added tax (VAT);
- accelerated privatisation;
- the withdrawal of the Reserve Bank from the forward cover market;
- International Monetary Fund assiatnce to help alleviate short-term pain caused by some of these measures.
-- Ben Hirschler, Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
